entries.meaning: Vaidehī met her beloved relatives, greeting each in the manner suited to that person. When everyone saw Jānakī in an ascetic's dress, an extraordinary anguish overwhelmed them. With the permission of Janaka, Rāma, and the guru, Sītā's parents came to where she was. Janaka drew Jānakī to his breast—the holy guest dearer to him than life. An ocean of love surged in his heart, and the king's mind became, as it were, Prayāga itself: there the banyan of affection for Sītā towered, adorned by the child of love for Rāma. It was as though an immortal sage, his knowledge confounded while drowning, had found an infant to support him. This was not delusion in the mind of the disembodied Videha, but the greatness of his love for Sītā and Raghubara. Sītā's mother became helpless under affection and could not compose herself; the daughter of Earth held firm by considering the occasion and her noble duty.

Seeing Sītā in an ascetic's dress gave Janaka an extraordinary mingling of love and contentment. He said, ‘Daughter, you have purified both your families; the whole world proclaims your stainless fame. The river of your renown has surpassed the Gaṅgā and coursed through countless cosmic eggs. The Gaṅgā has made only three places upon earth especially great, while yours has created dense assemblies of saints everywhere.’ At her father's truthful, loving words, Sītā seemed to withdraw into herself through reserve. Her father and mother embraced her again and gave lovely counsel, blessings, and good wishes. Sītā did not speak, but inwardly felt it would not be right to remain there that night. Reading her inclination, the queen informed the king while admiring her character. After meeting Sītā repeatedly, they honored her and took leave. At the proper moment the wise, eloquent queen also told the king of Bharata's condition.

When the king heard of Bharata's conduct, he felt that gold had acquired fragrance, nectar its quintessence, and the moon its finest radiance. He closed his tear-filled eyes, his body thrilled, and joyfully began praising Bharata's fair fame. ‘Listen attentively, lovely and fair-eyed queen: Bharata's story releases one from the bonds of becoming. According to my ability I can discourse here on duty, statecraft, and contemplation of Brahman; yet what power has that intellect to describe Bharata's greatness? Even by a trick it cannot touch its shadow. The Creator, Gaṇeśa, Śeṣa, Śiva, Sarasvatī, poets, scholars, sages, and masters of understanding cannot encompass Bharata's conduct, fame, deeds, duty, character, virtues, and stainless glory. To understand or hear of them gives joy to all; their purity is like the celestial river, while their sweetness puts nectar to shame. Bharata's virtues are boundless and the man himself beyond comparison. Calling even Mount Sumeru equal to a mere seer-weight would make every poet's intellect recoil in shame.’

Every syllable falters in attempting what is inaccessible to all, as a fish deprived of water cannot travel upon land. ‘Queen, hear of Bharata's limitless greatness: Rāma knows it, yet even he cannot fully tell it.’ After lovingly describing Bharata's spiritual power and seeing the desire in his wife's heart, the king said: ‘If Lakṣmaṇa returns and Bharata goes to the forest, it would satisfy everyone and benefit all. Yet the love and mutual trust between Bharata and Raghubara cannot be reached by inference. Bharata is the limit of affection and tender attachment, although Rāma is the boundary of impartiality. Bharata has never regarded the essence of either highest or personal good and happiness, even in a dream. For him love of Rāma's feet is both the means and the attainment—this is the judgment I discern in Bharata. Not even inadvertently would he press against Rāma's command, even in thought. Do not worry.’ The king spoke so under the power of affection and then lamented.

The royal couple passed the night counting Rāma's and Bharata's virtues with love, and it seemed no longer than the blink of an eye. At dawn both royal companies awoke and, after bathing, began worshiping the gods. Raghurāya bathed and went to the guru; bowing at his feet, he spoke when he saw the right disposition: ‘Lord, Bharata, the townspeople, and the mothers are afflicted by grief and distressed by my forest exile. The lord of Mithilā too, with his whole company, has endured hardship for many days. Please do what is fitting, Lord; everyone's welfare lies in your hands.’ Having said this, Raghurāya shrank deeply with reserve, and the sage thrilled to see his character and nature. The guru answered: ‘Without you, Rāma, every provision for happiness seems hellish to both royal companies. You are the life of their life, the soul of their soul, and the happiness within their happiness. Dear child, fate is hostile to those who find their homes pleasing after abandoning you.’

‘Let that happiness, action, and duty burn where there is no love for the lotus of Rāma's feet. So too with favorable or adverse discipline, knowledge or ignorance, wherever love for Rāma is not supreme. Without you all are miserable and through you they are happy; you know what lies within every heart. Your command rests upon everyone's head, and the Compassionate One knows each person's condition perfectly. Please return now to your hermitage.’ The sage-king's body had gone slack with affection. Rāma bowed and departed; the seer steadied himself and went to Janaka. He repeated Rāma's words to the king, lovely in character, affection, and natural grace, and said: ‘Great king, now do what will uphold everyone's duty and welfare. Wise, pure, steadfast ruler and treasury of knowledge, who but you can resolve this uncertainty at such a time?’

Hearing the sage's words, Janaka filled with love; at the sight of his condition, knowledge and detachment themselves seemed to renounce him. His body slack with affection, he thought: ‘It was not well that I came here. The king ordered Rāma to the forest and made his own life the proof of his love. Now we would send Rāma from one forest into another and return delighted, boasting of our discernment!’ The ascetics, sages, and brahmins who heard and saw this became extraordinarily helpless under love. Understanding the occasion, the king gathered his courage and went with the assembly to Bharata. Bharata came forward and received them, then offered seats suited to the occasion. ‘Dear Bharata,’ said the king of Tirhut, ‘you know Raghubīra's nature: Rāma is true to his vow, devoted to duty, and full of character and affection toward everyone. Constrained by reserve, he endures this crisis. Tell us what command you give.’

Hearing this, Bharata's body thrilled and his eyes filled with water. Mustering great courage, he replied: ‘My lord, you are beloved and venerable, like a father; neither mother nor father is so beneficial as you and the family guru. The sages headed by Kauśika, the assembly of ministers, and you yourself are today an ocean of wisdom. Regard me as a child and servant who follows commands, and instruct me, Lord. For you to question me before this assembly leaves me at a loss: silence would be sullen, yet for me to speak is foolish. With a small mouth I utter a great matter; forgive me, father, seeing that destiny is adverse. The Āgamas, Vedas, and Purāṇas famously declare that the duty of service is difficult in this world. A servant's duty opposes self-interest; enmity is blind, while love has no discriminating counsel. Keep Rāma's preference, duty, and vow foremost; regard me as dependent and, recognizing the love involved, do with everyone's assent whatever benefits all.’

Hearing Bharata's words and seeing his disposition, the king praised him along with the assembly. His speech was accessible yet unfathomable, gentle and charming yet firm, with limitless meaning in very few syllables. Like a face within a mirror and the mirror held in one's own hand, his astonishing words could be seen clearly but not grasped. The king and Bharata went with the sages and assembly to where Rāma, the moon to the water-lilies of the wise, was seated. Hearing what had happened, everyone became anxious, like schools of fish stirred by new water. The gods first observed the family guru's disposition; then they saw Videha's extraordinary affection. When they beheld Bharata wholly made of devotion to Rāma, the self-interested immortals trembled and lost heart. Everyone appeared filled with love for Rāma; the gods' fear was beyond reckoning, yet through worry it came into the account. Troubled by love and reserve between Rāma and Bharata, Indra said anxiously: ‘Join all five and weave an illusion; otherwise our purpose is lost.’

The gods remembered and extolled Sarasvatī: ‘Goddess, protect the gods who have sought your refuge. Use your own illusion to turn Bharata's mind, and shield the celestial race with the shadow of deception.’ Hearing their plea, the wise goddess recognized the immortals as selfish fools and replied: ‘You ask me to turn Bharata's mind? Though you have a thousand eyes, you fail to see Sumeru! Even the immensely powerful illusion of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva cannot so much as look upon that mind. In asking this of me you treat me as a simpleton. Can moonlight steal a ray from the fierce sun? Sītā and Rāma dwell in Bharata's heart; can darkness remain where the sun shines?’ Saying this, Sarasvatī went to Brahmā's realm, while the distressed gods became like cakravāka birds at night. With selfish and impure minds, they had contrived an evil counsel and a disastrous situation: their powerful illusion produced fear, confusion, disaffection, and restlessness.
